Abstract
A new approach for estimating the system response time (SRT) is presented and demonstrated through the analysis of the 
effect of target latitude on SRT, both with and without inter-satellite links (ISL). The access time intervals for each satellite 
to ground stations, targets, and between pairs of satellites are computed. The SRT for a target is calculated using a proposed 
algorithm that includes an adapted Dijkstra algorithm on a time-varying link graph for the ISLs. For the geospatial analysis, 
the average, minimum, and maximum SRTs of the targets of all SRTs were introduced as performance metrics. Combined 
with a visualization on a world map, this method allows us to quickly grasp the strengths and weaknesses of the constella-
tion with regards to SRT. When plotted as a function of latitude [− 90°, 90°], the SRT for constellations with and without 
ISL in mid and high-inclination orbits peaks at the equator and drops towards the Earth’s poles, influenced by the satellite 
constellation and ground station network design. ISLs smoothen the SRT curve and reduce the effect of the latitude, thereby 
enhancing data acquisition speed by minimizing SRT variation over time and across longitudes.
Keywords  Satellite constellation · System response time · Inter-satellite links · Geospatial analysis
1  Introduction
The rising demand for real-time availability of satellite 
Earth observation data has driven the development of large 
satellite constellations and technologies like inter-satellite 
links (ISL). Predicting the system response time (SRT) 
for satellite Earth observation data collected by a satellite 
constellation is, therefore, a crucial step in the design of 
a satellite constellation to guarantee its performance, cost-
efficiency, and sustainability. The SRT is defined here as 
the time interval between a user’s data collection request 
for Earth observation imagery ( t0 ) from an arbitrary target 
point on Earth and the receipt of the requested data ( tSRT ) 
at the user’s location through the satellite constellation and 
its ground stations.
Previous studies have optimized Earth-observing satel-
lite constellations for metrics such as average revisit time 
[1, 2] and coverage duration [3]. Kim and Chang [4] have 
developed heuristic algorithms for optimization of the con-
stellation operation with regards to the SRT of an Earth 
Observation constellation. Sanad [5] analyzes the SRT of 
Earth observation satellite constellations that use relay com-
munication satellite constellations. He computes the SRT 
via the intrinsic response time (i.e., time between a satel-
lites’ uplink and target access) and average time gaps but 
does not calculate the SRT for specific time points of user 
requests. Chan [6] examines how ISLs and satellite propul-
sion help reducing the SRT in Earth observation satellite 
constellations.
The reduction of SRT with ISLs was examined by De 
Florio [7]. In this work, only one ground station was consid-
ered, and no geospatial analysis was performed. The work of 
Scherberger et al. [8] presents a general method to compute 
the SRT over mission time and for global targets for satellite 
constellations; however, without considering ISLs. In Ref. 
[9], the ISL paths of mega-constellations were analyzed. The 
number of ISLs for transmitting information between two 
ground locations is called hop-count. Its spatial distribution 
is theoretically estimated and shown in an example.
In none of the above studies, the effect of target lati-
tude on SRT with ISLs has been analyzed. This analysis is

the SRT as well as the minimum and maximum SRTs. We 
demonstrate this method by examining Walker constella-

the commercial ground station network of Kongsberg Satel-

2  Method
In this section, a method for calculating the SRT of satel-
lite constellation with inter-satellite communication links 
is introduced. After outlining the assumptions (2.1), the 
general method for computing the SRT is described (2.2), 
followed by an algorithmic specification to consider ISLs. 
The method builds on Ref. [8], where an algorithm for com-
puting the SRT of a satellite constellation was proposed that 
does not consider ISLs.
2.1  Assumptions
The model makes the following assumptions. Ground sta-
tions are permanently available, and every ground station 
allows simultaneous uplink and downlink, ignoring schedul-
ing issues. Satellite sensors are also permanently available, 
supporting uplink and downlink simultaneously; possible 
energy constraints are ignored. Moreover, storage con-
straints of onboard data in satellites are ignored. Latencies 
for uplink and downlink transmission of data are neglected. 
It is assumed that no satellite will appear multiple times 
in a ISL path between uplink and target access or between 
target access and downlink. Hence, the number of ISLs 
between uplink and target access or between target access 
and downlink is limited each to a maximum of Lmax = N −1 
links, where N is the number of satellites, and Lmax is the 
maximum number of ISLs. In most practical situations of 
our analysis, L , the actual link number, is much smaller 
than Lmax . In addition, for the presented data, a connection 
between a satellite and a ground station is assumed to be 
possible if the satellite exceeds a minimum elevation angle 
above the horizon of the ground station. An ISL between 
a pair of satellites is assumed to be possible if they are in 
line of sight. The analysis time of the presented data was 
1 month with an arbitrarily selected time step of 50 s, so one 
SRT value is obtained for every 50 s within this 1 month. 
Only LEO satellite constellations where all satellites have 
the same altitude were considered in the presented data.
2.2  Framing the SRT algorithm into a method
To obtain a global and time-independent understanding of 
the SRT behavior, it is necessary to calculate the SRT for 
different parameters. This is accomplished using the method 
described in Ref. [8], which is briefly outlined along with its 
application in this work:
As a first step, the access time intervals for each satellite 
to ground stations, targets, and between pairs of satellites 
are computed (Fig. 1). The implementation details will be 
explained in subSect. 2.4. Next, a Monte-Carlo simulation 
is performed for the targets. For the results of this work, 500 
targets were sampled from a random uniform distribution on 
the Earth’s surface. The analysis time interval is discretized 
into equidistant time points, i.e., separated by a constant time 
step, to model a user’s request for a sensor measurement at 
each time point and target. Time points with a time step of 
50 seconds over a mission time of 1 month were chosen for 
the produced results of this work. Section 3 shows the results 
for a 1-month mission time, which are almost identical to 
those for a 2-week mission time. This suggests that the cho-
sen mission time is sufficiently long. For each time point and 
every target, the SRT is computed by an adapted Dijkstra 
algorithm which will be described in the next subsection. 
Specifically, if the SRT is known for a user’s request at a 
time point t0 and has an uplink time tup , then the absolute 
downlink time is the same for all time points between t0 
and tup , and the SRT does not need to be calculated again 
for those time points. That is why the current time point is 
increased to the next uplink time in the arrow going back-
wards in the flow diagram (Fig. 1). Moreover, the minimum 
elevation angle above the horizon at which a satellite can 
establish a connection with a ground station is an input but 
set to 5° for simplicity in the results of this work (Table 2). 
The minimum elevation angle above the horizon at which a 
satellite can access a target is set to 10°. By calculating the 
average, minimum, and maximum SRTs (along the discrete

2.3  Algorithm for predicting the SRT with ISLs
This section presents the algorithm for calculating the SRT 
of a user request for data acquisition from a specific target at 
a specific time, given the access intervals from all satellites 
to ground stations and targets as well as between satellite 
pairs (for ISLs). This is represented by the two blocks within 
the “for” loop in Fig. 1.
To compute the SRT, the next access to a ground object, 
such as a target or a ground station, must be found which 
corresponds to the minimal access time (absolute time) a 
satellite can reach. Calculating the next access from a satel-
lite to a ground station or a target at a time point based on a 
given list of access intervals can be done using an adapted 
binary search [8].
A satellite network consists of satellites and ISLs as com-
munication connections between them. Satellite networks 
are very time dynamic because satellites that can establish 
a ISL at one moment might not be able to have a ISL a few 
minutes later. This motivates the usage of a time-varying 
graph to model this network. In our context, each satellite 
is represented by a node and each ordered pair of satellites 
is represented by a directed edge with time-varying weight. 
The weight of an edge for a given time point represents the 
time interval from the given time until the next link is possi-
ble. To state this in a graph theory notation, let the set of ver-
tices V be the set of all satellites, i.e., V = {sat1, … , satN} . 
Let T = ℝ≥0 ∪{∞} be a time space for all times after a 
start time. Let the set of edges E be the set of all satellite 
pairs, i.e., E = V × V . The time-varying weight function 
w ∶E × T →T  maps an edge (satellite pair) at a specific 
time to the duration of the time interval from the given time 
until the next time the satellite pair can communicate. A con-
structive definition is given in Eq. (2) after developing more 
formalization. Then G = (V, E, w) is the directed, weighted, 
and time-varying graph used here.
To consider ISLs for the SRT calculation, a modified 
version of Dijkstra’s algorithm is applied to a weighted, 
directed, and time-varying graph. Dijkstra’s algorithm is a 
graph theory algorithm that calculates the shortest route in a 
network [13]. For instance, the classical Dijkstra’s algorithm 
can determine the route with the shortest distance from a 
starting point in a street network to all destinations in a cer-
tain neighborhood, where the start and end destinations are 
nodes, the streets are edges, and the street distances are the 
edge weights. However, this classical Dijkstra’s algorithm 
must be adapted for the time-varying graph used here. In the 
context of the street network example, the modified Dijkstra 
algorithm can minimize the travel time from A to B in a 
street network where the travel time on a street may vary

over time due to factors like traffic. Delivering informa-
tion as fast as possible from a starting point to an end point 
in a time-varying routing network is known as the earliest 
delivery problem [11]. An adapted Dijkstra algorithm with 
a time-varying and directed cost function can solve this ear-
liest delivery problem [11]. In Ref. [6], this algorithm is 
mentioned in the context of satellite routing. We want to 
use this algorithm to compute the system response time of 
satellite constellations with ISLs.
To obtain the SRT, two ISL routing problems must be 
solved: determining how to link between satellites after an 
uplink to the target and how to link between satellites from 
the target to the downlink. A priori, it is not known which 
satellite will be used for uplink and which satellite will be 
used for target access to ensure that the ISL path results in 
a minimal SRT. Hence, the start and end nodes for these 
two routing problems are not clearly defined and different 
initializations must be considered in our approach.
To consider a satellite’s energy and technical ISL con-
straints, we introduce the maximum number of ISLs per 
data package (such as requests or measurement data) as a 
parameter in the SRT calculation with ISLs. Hence, there 
is only a maximum number of ISLs considered for each the 
ISLs between uplink and target access as well as the ISLs 
between target access and downlink in our model. In Ref. 
[11], a modified Dijkstra’s algorithm for time-varying edge 
costs is presented (see algorithm 1 of Ref. [11]). We extend 
this algorithm by specifying the cost function for our appli-
cation and by introducing an upper bound for the number of 
ISLs. This modification ensures that only ISLs paths within 
the specified bound are considered, thereby maintaining the 
algorithm’s validity and optimality. The modifications com-
pared to algorithm 1 in Ref. [11] are shown in Fig. 2. The 
adapted Dijkstra algorithm computes the next possible ISL 
from a selected node to each of the remaining nodes which 
are still unvisited, i.e., still an element of Q (Fig. 2).
At its core, Dijkstra’s algorithm iteratively explores an 
expanding neighborhood of nodes starting from the initial 
node. As a side note, this neighborhood of (already visited) 
nodes is here the set of all nodes that were removed from Q . 
For a set of already visited nodes, Q is the set of all nodes, 
each paired with the minimal distances that they can be 
reached from the start node via the current neighborhood 
and one extra edge. Practically, Q is implemented as a pri-
ority queue (special data structure) where the correspond-
ing distances (i.e., sums of edge costs) of each node is the 
priority value. In Fig. 2, for each node n , the sum of all 
edge weights along the (so far) shortest path from the start 
node to the node n is stored in pathDistance. During each 
iteration, a new node u is considered which has the minimal 
value in pathDistance of all nodes in Q . Furthermore, dur-
ing each iteration, where a new node u is considered, the 
algorithm updates the sum of all edge weights along the (so 
far) shortest path from the start node to the node n in Q if a 
smaller one is found. The algorithm terminates after check-
ing all possible paths in an efficient way. Moreover, keeping 
track of the visited nodes in the for loop in Fig. 2 yields the 
path of ISLs.
Before explaining the adapted Dijkstra algorithm in our 
practical context, we will discuss how SRTs are computed 
with the adapted Dijkstra algorithm which is illustrated in 
Fig. 3, where purple arrows between two satellites repre-
sent potential ISL chains, so potentially multiple ISLs via 
other satellites. Arrows between a ground station and a sat-
ellite represent a direct uplink or a downlink without any 
ISLs in between. All ISL chains symbolized by the outgo-
ing arrows marked by one Dijkstra sign are computed by 
applying the adapted Dijkstra algorithm for time-varying 
networks once. The adapted Dijkstra algorithm inputs a 
start satellite. Since it is unknown a priori which satellite 
will first access a ground object, each satellite is treated 
as a start satellite (Fig. 3). For each start satellite, the fast-
est link paths to all other satellites within the maximum 
number of ISLs from the start satellite are calculated by 
applying the adapted Dijkstra algorithm once and add-
ing the resulting time with the additional time required to 
access the next ground object. Consequently, for each of 
the two routing problems, the adapted Dijkstra algorithm 
is applied N times where N is the number of satellites 
(Fig. 3). The function nextAccess in Fig. 3 will be formally 
defined in Eq. (1). As previously mentioned, different link 
paths must be considered. For each state, such as a satel-
lite after uplink, before target access, or before downlink, 
the ISL path requiring the least time to reach that state is 
selected. This is represented by the red min in Fig. 3.

The goal of the adapted Dijkstra algorithm (Fig. 4) is to 
find the next access to one target (or ground station) using 
ISLs after a start time, beginning from the start satellite. 
This is illustrated in Fig. 4 where Satellite 1 is the start sat-
ellite. Note the vertical time axis in Fig. 4, which begins at 
the start time. The thin arrows represent the ISLs between 
satellites and are the weighted edges of the network consid-
ered for Dijkstra’s algorithm. The edge weights in Fig. 4 are 
chosen arbitrary but based on a realistic magnitude for such 
values. The ability to perform an ISL is most of the time 
bidirectional, but the arrow only indicates the exploration 
steps taken in this example. The single target is represented 
in blue, but it is shown separately for each satellite because 
the access time, and therefore its position on the vertical 
time axis, can differ for each satellite. Starting from Satellite 
1, the time intervals required for the next links are calcu-
lated, identifying the adjacent nodes, and allowing Dijkstra’s 
algorithm to proceed with its next step.
Dijkstra’s algorithm constructs a minimal spanning tree 
(in a graph theory sense) of all satellites in the neighborhood 
where the paths along the tree from the start node to every 
node represent the shortest route. Consequently, the pro-
posed algorithm always finds the shortest link path to every 
satellite. In Fig. 4, the red arrows represent this minimal 
spanning tree since the minimal time distance from satel-
lite 1 to 2 is 5 min, from satellite 1 to 3 is 5 min + 15 min 
and from satellite 1 to 4 is 5 min + 15 min + 0 min. After 
calculating the minimal time and path for the next link from 
satellite 1 to every other satellite, the access time for the next 
target (or ground station) for each satellite can be determined 
based on the times at which each satellite is reached by ISLs. 
These times are represented by the blue arrows pointing to 
the targets. Hence, it is only necessary to minimize over all 
satellites to receive the minimal access time to one target 
from satellite 1 with ISLs. The ISL paths are outputted in 
addition to the SRTs.

2.4  Implementation
The framework of this method is implemented in Python, 
utilizing the following tools for orbital mechanics as men-
tioned in Fig. 1: The Python library Skyfield is employed 
to compute the access intervals between the satellites and 
targets or ground stations [14, 15]. For calculating access 
intervals between satellites, Ansys’ System Tool Kit (STK) 
version 2023 R3 is used, accessed through STK’s Python 
API [16].
Most of the computation time of the SRT algorithm is 
dedicated to computing the access intervals between satel-
lites and ground stations or targets as well as between all 
pairs of satellites. The SRT algorithm exhibits a quadratic 
runtime with respect to the number of satellites but linear 
complexity in relation to the number of ground stations, the 
number of targets and the mission time.
2.5  Demonstration examples
Walker constellations are satellite constellations where sat-
ellites are nearly evenly distributed around the Earth, pro-
viding a representative view of general constellations. The 
parameters of a Walker constellation are denoted as I : t / 
p / f  , where I represents the inclination of all satellites, t 
represents the total number of satellites, p represents the 
number of equally spaced planes, and f the relative spacing 
between satellites in adjacent planes [17]. For this notation, 
there are two kinds of Walker constellations: Walker delta 
and Walker star.
Demonstration examples for satellite constellations with 
an altitude of 500 km:
a)	 Walker star constellation 60°: 16 / 4 / 1 (Fig. 5) with 
KSAT ground stations
b)	 Walker delta constellation 97.4°: 9 / 1 / 1 (Fig. 6) with 
ground stations in Tromsø (Norway) and Punta Arenas 
(Chile)

quantile is defined as the smallest value x ∈ℝ such that at 
least a fraction p of the values in R are less or equal to x , 
i.e., Q(p) = min{x ∈ℝ∶F(x) ≥p} . Specifically, it holds 
that Q(0) = min(R) and Q(1) = max(R) . In our analysis, we 
will state p in percent and computeQ(20%), Q(40%), Q(60%)
, Q(80%), Q(100%) . This allows to state the distribution of 
the values of R.

Figure 7 shows the SRT without ISLs (left) and with 
ISLs (right) over target latitude for constellation (b). Each 
of the 500 modeled targets is represented by one colored 
point in Fig. 7, whereas its latitude is encoded by the x-value 
and the longitude is encoded by the color of the point. The 
y-value of each colored point represents the average SRT 
of the corresponding target. The variation of the SRT over 
mission time for each target, ranging from the minimum to 
the maximum SRT for each target, is indicated by the black 
variation bar attached to the colored point for the average 
SRT. In Fig. 7, the sun-synchronous constellation (b) was 
used such that all targets at the poles are regularly accessed 
and all values can be shown within the SRT axis.
Contrary to Fig. 7, a medium-inclined satellite constella-
tion is used in Fig. 8. Therefore, some targets with a latitude 
of at least 75° cannot be accessed or can only be accessed 
very rarely with 60° inclined satellites (Fig. 5). Hence, such

limits in Fig. 8 are set such that 95% of the max SRT val-

Both without and with ISLs, the average and maximum 
SRT peaks at targets positioned near the equator and drops 
towards the Earth’s poles (Figs. 7, 8). The SRT curve over 
target latitude without ISLs and especially with ISLs has 
a bell-shaped appearance, both for satellite constellations 
with medium (Fig. 8) and high (Fig. 7) inclinations. The 
average SRT without ISLs has a variation of approximately 
1 h (Fig. 7 left) and 0.5 h (Fig. 8 left) at the equator. On 
the other side, the average SRT with ISLs has a variation 
of smaller than 0.1 h (Fig. 7 right) and 0.1 h (Fig. 8 right). 
The variation of the maximum SRT is reduced from 2 h to 
0.5 h in Fig. 7 as well as from up to 1.5 h to up to 0.5 h in 
Fig. 8 with ISLs. While some minimum SRT values without 
ISLs are greater than 1.5 h, the minimum SRT is close to 
0 h for all targets (Fig. 7). This SRT curve over latitude is 
more symmetric with ISLs (Figs. 7, 8). As expected, ISLs 
significantly reduce the average, minimum, and especially 
maximum SRT (Figs. 7, 8).
Figures 7 and 8 show the range of SRT values, from 
minimum to maximum, which is quite broad. However, the 
distribution of SRT values cannot be deduced from Figs. 7 
and 8. To examine the distribution of SRT values between 
the minimum and maximum, the quantiles of all the SRT 
data points for each target over target latitude are shown in 
Figs. 9 and 10. As mentioned in Sect. 2.6, the 100% quantile

Consider the SRT over latitude without ISLs in Fig. 9

quantile of the SRT (denoted by Q(20%) ) is between 1.7 h 
and 2.1 h depending on the longitude of the target. There-

are less than approximately 2 h. Because the SRT values 
were obtained for discrete equidistant time points, we can 
say that the SRT is smaller than approximately 2 h in 20% 
of the time. Analogously, the SRT is smaller than 8.5 h to 
9.5 h for targets at the equator, depending on target longi-

and Q(60%) are exactly 20% of the data points. In Fig. 9, 
the quantiles are approximately equally spaced, i.e., the 
SRT is distributed homogeneously between the minimum 
and maximum.
Even for targets with the same latitude, the value of a 
quantile can vary depending on the target’s longitude. In 
Fig. 9, the 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% quantiles for the SRT 
without ISLs each vary by about 1 h for targets with the 
same latitude but different longitudes. This variation is 
reduced to 0.1 h in the case with ISLs (Fig. 9). In Fig. 10, 
the quantiles vary more, i.e., are much more vertically 
spread out, but ISLs still reduce the ISL variation signifi-
cantly. In Fig. 10, the 20% quantile is almost 0, i.e., the 
SRT is almost zero in 20% of the time with constellation

closer to 0 h in Fig. 10, especially with ISLs, compared to 
Fig. 9, even when considering relative differences. Hence, 
the quantiles are still continuously distributed over the 
complete range from minimum to maximum, but this dis-
tribution has a high density at 0. One reason for this is 
that constellation (a) has a bigger ground station network.
Combining the results of Figs. 7, 8, 9, 10, the variation 
of ISLs for targets of the same latitude decreases when 
using ISLs, i.e., ISLs smooth the SRT curve over latitude. 
As a result of that, ISLs can compensate for an unbalanced 
positioning of ground stations over latitude. One natural 
reason of an unbalanced positioning of ground stations is 
that the majority of the Earth’s landmass is on the Northern 
Hemisphere.

on a world map offers a simple method to evaluate a satellite 
constellation with its ground station network with respect to 
the SRT. This allows the easy identification of regions where 
the constellation performs well or poorly. This can be used 
to optimize a constellation during the design phase.
In Fig. 12, the global average SRT, i.e., the mean SRT 
averaged over 500 targets, is shown. Hence, each data point 
in Fig. 12 represents the average over all 500 targets with 
each over 50,000 time points for which the SRT was com-
puted. The constellation (b) is chosen for this because it 
offers a permanent link availability for neighboring satellites 
on the same plane, which allows many ISLs, while maintain-
ing a limited number of ground stations, thus enhancing the 
clarity of ISL effects. The first few ISLs influences SRT the 
most, according to Fig. 12. This behavior is consistent with 
the findings in Ref. [9] about the number of ISLs needed 
in a mega-constellation for connecting two ground stations 
which is called hop-number and a closely related metric.
4  Conclusion
A new method has been developed that allows the efficient 
computation of SRT with ISL. This method was applied 
to compute the SRT for two Earth observation constella-
tion types and randomly distributed targets worldwide. The 
results show that target latitude has a much greater influence 
on SRT than target longitude. The average and maximum 
SRT curves peak at the equator and drop towards the poles 
when plotted against target latitude. Furthermore, the results 
demonstrate that including ISLs significantly smooths the 
average SRT over different latitudes, thereby compensating 
for the effects of longitude variations. ISLs reduce SRT vari-
ations and enhance data acquisition speed by minimizing 
SRT variation over time and across longitudes, providing a 
more symmetric SRT distribution towards the equator. This 
improvement is especially beneficial in compensating for the 
unbalanced positioning of ground stations due to the uneven 
distribution of Earth’s landmass.

Abstract: A new approach for estimating the system response time (SRT) is presented and demonstrated through the analysis of the effect of target latitude on SRT, both with and without inter-satellite links (ISL). The access time intervals for each satellite to ground stations, targets, and between pairs of satellites are computed. The SRT for a target is calculated using a proposed algorithm that includes an adapted Dijkstra algorithm on a time-varying link graph for the ISLs. For the geospatial analysis, the average, minimum, and maximum SRTs of the targets of all SRTs were introduced as performance metrics. Combined with a visualization on a world map, this method allows us to quickly grasp the strengths and weaknesses of the constella- tion with regards to SRT. When plotted as a function of latitude [− 90°, 90°], the SRT for constellations with and without ISL in mid and high-inclination orbits peaks at the equator and drops towards the Earth’s poles, influenced by the satellite constellation and ground station network design. ISLs smoothen the SRT curve and reduce the effect of the latitude, thereby enhancing data acquisition speed by minimizing SRT variation over time and across longitudes.
